<reason>B (CON) won a clear but competitive debate. Both sides obeyed the Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure and engaged the live clash. B's two decisive moves were: (1) the consent-symmetry trap in B2.1 — if defaults shape behavior when PRO sets them, "accept all" buttons were consent too — which A answered only with the reversible-switch asymmetry, and B4.2 countered that statutory lock-in differs from market-punishable defaults; and (2) B4.3's narrow-vs-maximal distinction: Safari/Firefox shipped only third-party cookie limits, not "robust ad and tracker blocking" as the motion requires, which defused A's strongest empirical analogy and exposed A's quiet narrowing of the mandate from ad blocking to tracker-only blocking. B also landed the economics gap (contextual ads at fractions of behavioral revenue) that A never repaired beyond reassertion, and correctly corrected A's school-device claim via MDM. A's strongest material — the "choose the switch" framing, the in-app webview/coverage gap, and the TLS/patch-cycle answer to the frozen-law charge — kept the debate close, but A left the funding question and the scope mismatch unanswered. B's clipped opening is a minor execution cost. B made the debate easier to decide with consistent calibration-vs-sweeping weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.3's distinction that Safari and Firefox shipped narrow tracking prevention (funded partly by search-ad deals) rather than the robust system-level ad blocking the motion mandates, which neutralized A's "those defaults didn't collapse free services" pressure question and became the spine of B's closing.</best_rebuttal>
